# Areté — academic companion for the University of Uyo

> ἀρετή (ar-eh-TAY). A free study companion for University of Uyo undergraduates in Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria: the outline, recommended textbooks and study tips for all 95 courses from 100 Level to Final Year, transcribed lecture notes and past-paper practice for a growing set of them, interactive Java, Python and C tracks, a capture-the-flag security track, and an AI tutor that has read the curriculum.

- Site: https://www.aretecyb.tech
- Institution: University of Uyo (https://www.uniuyo.edu.ng/, https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q7896523)
- Audience: 100 Level – 400 Level undergraduates
- Departments with a fully authored catalogue: Cybersecurity, Data Science. Every other department gets the shared GST, MTH, PHY, STA, COS, CSC, ENT and INS courses.
- Access: course outlines, textbooks and study tips are public. Lecture notes, question banks, the AI tutor and progress tracking need a free account (email code, no password).
- Last generated: 2026-09-08


## 100 Level

### COS 111 — Introduction to Computing Sciences

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cos-111
- 3 units · 100 Level · First Semester

A broad survey of the computing field: hardware, software, human-ware, information processing, and the many specializations within computing. Lays the conceptual vocabulary and hands-on device familiarity for everything that follows in your degree.

**Outline**

1. Brief history of computing
2. Basic components of a computer/computing device; input/output devices and peripherals
3. Hardware, software and human-ware
4. Diverse and growing computer/digital applications
5. Information processing and its role in society
6. The Internet: applications and impact on the world today
7. Areas and specializations within the computing discipline; job specializations for computing professionals
8. The future of computing
9. Lab work: OS across desktops/laptops/tablets/phones, common applications, browsers, search engines, online resources

**Recommended textbooks**

- Introduction to Computers and Information Technology — Gary B. Shelly & Misty E. Vermaat
- Computer Science: An Overview — J. Glenn Brookshear & Dennis Brylow

**How to pass**

- This is the course that sets the tone — learn number conversions until they are automatic
- CrashCourse Computer Science on YouTube (free) covers most of this course in engaging 10-minute episodes
- Harvard CS50 (free on edX) is the gold standard introduction to computing — bookmark it
- Link every abstract concept to something physical: binary → two states of a switch/transistor

### GST 111 — Communication in English

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/gst-111
- 2 units · 100 Level · First Semester

Develops the English language skills required for academic and professional success: sound patterns, word classes, sentence construction, logical/critical reasoning, and writing craft. A foundation course that improves every other course you will take.

**Outline**

1. Sound patterns in English: vowels, consonants, phonetics and phonology
2. Word classes: lexical and grammatical words, forms and usage
3. Sentence types: structural, functional, simple and complex
4. Grammar and usage: tense, mood, modality, and concord
5. Logical and critical thinking: syllogism, inductive and deductive reasoning, analogy
6. Ethical considerations, copyright rules and infringements
7. Writing process: pre-writing, drafting, editing and proofreading; essays, CVs, reports
8. Comprehension strategies and reading types
9. ICT in modern language learning; public speaking and listening

**Recommended textbooks**

- Communicating in English — Aremo, Adetayo & Farinde
- English Grammar in Use — Raymond Murphy

**How to pass**

- Do not treat GST courses as unimportant — writing skills affect your grades in every other course
- Practice essay writing by timing yourself: 45 minutes per essay, as you will in the exam
- Build vocabulary by reading one news article daily and noting unfamiliar words
- Keep a small notebook of common grammar errors you make and review it weekly

### MTH 111 — Elementary Mathematics I (Algebra and Trigonometry)

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/mth-111
- 2 units · 100 Level · First Semester

Algebra and trigonometry for university-level computation: set theory, real and complex numbers, sequences and series, quadratic equations, and circular measure. Bridges secondary-school maths with the rigour needed for the programme.

**Outline**

1. Elementary set theory: subsets, union, intersection, complements, Venn diagrams
2. Real numbers: integers, rational and irrational numbers, mathematical induction
3. Real sequences and series
4. Theory of quadratic equations and the binomial theorem
5. Complex numbers: algebra of complex numbers, the Argand diagram
6. De Moivre's theorem and nth roots of unity
7. Circular measure and trigonometric functions of angles of any magnitude
8. Addition and factor formulae

**Recommended textbooks**

- Engineering Mathematics — K.A. Stroud
- Further Mathematics — Tuttuh-Adegun, Sivasubramaniam & Adegoke

**How to pass**

- Work at least 10 practice problems per topic — mathematics is only learnt by doing
- Keep a formula sheet and update it every week; review before each lecture
- Khan Academy is free and covers every topic in this course at the right level
- Form a study group: explaining a solution to a classmate reveals whether you truly understand it

### PHY 111 — General Physics I (Mechanics)

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/phy-111
- 2 units · 100 Level · First Semester

Classical mechanics: vectors, kinematics, Newtonian dynamics, conservation principles, rotational motion, and gravitation. Builds the physical intuition that underpins electronics, networking signals, and the hardware concepts met in later computing courses.

**Outline**

1. Space, time, units and dimensions; vectors and scalars
2. Differentiation of vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration; kinematics
3. Newton's laws of motion: inertial frames, impulse, momentum conservation
4. Equations of motion and application of Newtonian mechanics
5. Conservation principles: conservative forces, kinetic and potential energy
6. System of particles, centre of mass, rotational motion and torque
7. Angular momentum, polar coordinates, circular motion, moments of inertia
8. Gravitation: Newton's Law of Gravitation, Kepler's Laws, escape velocity, satellite orbits

**Recommended textbooks**

- University Physics with Modern Physics — Young & Freedman
- Fundamentals of Physics — Halliday, Resnick & Walker

**How to pass**

- Always draw a free-body diagram before attempting any mechanics problem
- Learn units and dimensions first — dimensional analysis catches most errors
- Connect physics concepts to real technology: waves → WiFi signals, thermodynamics → CPU cooling
- Khan Academy Physics covers this entire course for free — use it alongside lectures

### PHY 117 — General Practical Physics I

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/phy-117
- 1 unit · 100 Level · First Semester

Laboratory practicals that accompany PHY 111. Quantitative measurement, treatment of measurement errors, and graphical analysis across mechanical, electrical, light, heat, and viscosity experiments. Develops precision, scientific method, and report-writing discipline.

**Outline**

1. Laboratory safety and quantitative measurement techniques
2. Treatment of measurement errors
3. Studies of meters and the oscilloscope
4. Mechanical systems experiments
5. Electrical and mechanical resonant systems
6. Light, heat, and viscosity experiments
7. Graphical analysis of experimental data
8. Scientific report writing

**Recommended textbooks**

- Practical Physics — G.L. Squires
- Experimental Physics — R.A. Dunlap

**How to pass**

- Take measurements three times and average them — always follow good experimental practice
- Write up your lab report on the same day as the experiment while it is fresh in your memory
- Show all calculations clearly — marks in practicals are awarded for method, not just the answer
- Understand the theory behind each experiment before you arrive at the lab

### STA 111 — Descriptive Statistics

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/sta-111
- 3 units · 100 Level · First Semester

The language of data: types, sources, and methods of data collection; presentation, errors and approximations; and the core measures used to summarise a dataset. A foundation for every analysis task in research and data-driven decision-making.

**Outline**

1. Statistical data: types, sources and methods of collection
2. Presentation of data: tables, charts and graphs
3. Errors and approximations
4. Frequency and cumulative distributions
5. Measures of location: mean, median, mode
6. Measures of partition and dispersion: range, variance, standard deviation
7. Skewness and kurtosis
8. Rates, ratios and index numbers

**Recommended textbooks**

- Statistics for Management and Economics — Gerald Keller
- Introductory Statistics — Neil A. Weiss

**How to pass**

- StatQuest with Josh Starmer on YouTube makes every stats concept intuitive — start there
- Always choose the right measure of central tendency: mean for symmetric data, median for skewed data
- Practice calculating variance and standard deviation by hand at least 5 times before the exam
- Draw histograms and box plots manually — you see patterns that summary numbers hide

### UUY-CSC 111 — Computer Operations

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-csc-111
- 2 units · 100 Level · First Semester

Practical computer skills: laboratory safety, hardware components, operating system navigation, productivity software, internet operations, and an introduction to statistical computing with SPSS. The hands-on companion to COS 111.

**Outline**

1. Laboratory ethics and safety precautions; basic components of a computer system
2. Booting a PC; Windows, Unix, Linux and Macintosh operating systems
3. File systems: directories, subdirectories and file paths
4. Application packages: Word, Excel, Access, PowerPoint, CorelDraw
5. Internet operations: web browsers, e-mail, search engines
6. Document creation, editing, formatting and printing
7. Modern statistical computing and data management; verifying and transferring data
8. Introduction to SPSS: summarising data, hypothesis testing, correlation, regression, and probability distributions

**Recommended textbooks**

- Microsoft Office 365: In Practice — Randy Nordell
- Computer Literacy for IC3 — Connie Morrison & Faithe Wempen

**How to pass**

- Practise every application feature you learn immediately on your own computer
- Learn Excel functions early — VLOOKUP, SUMIF, and pivot tables appear in research projects later
- Touch-type practice daily (use keybr.com free) — speed matters more than you expect
- Save all your university work to Google Drive or OneDrive so nothing is ever lost

### UUY-CSC 112 — Computer Troubleshooting

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-csc-112
- 2 units · 100 Level · First Semester

Diagnosing and resolving common hardware and software problems across PCs, laptops, tablets, and mobile phones. Covers network connectivity/security troubleshooting, backup and restore, and virus/anti-virus procedures — practical skills every computing professional needs.

**Outline**

1. Fundamentals of hardware
2. Handling, testing and troubleshooting personal computer problems
3. Diagnosis and repair of laptops, tablets and mobile phones
4. Internet connections, network services, and network security troubleshooting
5. Maintenance of computer networks and peripherals
6. System backup and restore operations
7. Viruses and anti-virus procedures
8. Inbuilt and external diagnostic tools; installing, configuring, optimizing and upgrading systems

**Recommended textbooks**

- CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) — Mike Meyers
- PC Maintenance and Repair — Jean Andrews

**How to pass**

- Professor Messer on YouTube has a free, comprehensive CompTIA A+ course that covers this entire course
- When troubleshooting, always follow a systematic approach: most common cause → less common
- Build a habit of documenting every problem and its solution — this is how senior technicians work
- If you can access a spare PC to disassemble and reassemble, do it until it is routine

### UUY-DTS 111 — Fundamentals of Data Science

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-111
- 3 units · 100 Level · First Semester

Your orientation to the discipline: what data science actually is, what a data scientist does day to day, and the end-to-end lifecycle of a data project from question to deployed insight. Heavily practical — you will handle real datasets in your first semester.

**Outline**

1. What data science is: the intersection of statistics, computing and domain knowledge
2. Roles in the field: data analyst, data scientist, data engineer, ML engineer
3. The data science lifecycle: problem framing, collection, cleaning, exploration, modelling, communication, deployment
4. Types of data: structured, semi-structured and unstructured; quantitative vs qualitative
5. Data sources: surveys, sensors, transactions, logs, web scraping, open data portals
6. Data quality: missing values, duplicates, outliers, inconsistent coding
7. Exploratory data analysis and basic visualisation
8. Tools of the trade: spreadsheets, Python/R notebooks, SQL, version control
9. Case studies of data science in health, agriculture, finance and government in Nigeria

**Recommended textbooks**

- Data Science from Scratch — Joel Grus
- R for Data Science — Hadley Wickham & Garrett Grolemund
- Doing Data Science — Cathy O'Neil & Rachel Schutt

**How to pass**

- Pick one real dataset in your first month (Nigeria open data, NBS, or a Kaggle set) and carry it through every stage of the lifecycle as you learn each stage
- Cleaning is 70–80% of real data work and is barely 10% of the syllabus — over-invest in it anyway
- Start a public GitHub repository now; by 400 Level it is the portfolio that gets you hired
- Learn to state the business question before touching the data — an elegant model answering the wrong question scores zero

### UUY-DTS 112 — Introduction to Database Technology

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-112
- 2 units · 100 Level · First Semester

How data is stored, structured and retrieved at scale. Relational modelling, normalisation, and SQL — the single most reusable practical skill in the degree, and the one most often tested in data-science job interviews.

**Outline**

1. File systems vs database systems; why databases exist
2. Database system architecture: the three-schema architecture and data independence
3. Data models: hierarchical, network, relational, object and document models
4. Entity-relationship modelling: entities, attributes, relationships, cardinality, ER diagrams
5. The relational model: relations, tuples, keys (primary, candidate, foreign), integrity constraints
6. Normalisation: functional dependency, 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF
7. SQL data definition: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, constraints
8. SQL data manipulation: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, JOIN, subqueries, aggregate functions
9. Transactions and the ACID properties; introduction to NoSQL alternatives

**Recommended textbooks**

- Database System Concepts — Silberschatz, Korth & Sudarshan
- Learning SQL — Alan Beaulieu

**How to pass**

- Install PostgreSQL or SQLite locally in week one and write real queries — SQL cannot be learnt by reading
- Normalisation questions are guaranteed in the exam: practise taking an unnormalised table to 3NF and stating the functional dependency that forced each step
- Master JOINs properly (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL) — they are the number one SQL interview topic and reappear in DTS 314
- SQLBolt and pgexercises.com are free, interactive, and better practice than any past question paper

### COS 121 — Problem Solving

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cos-121
- 3 units · 100 Level · Second Semester

Algorithmic thinking and systematic problem solving using Python and C. Covers problem identification, solution techniques, pseudocode/flowcharts, and programming fundamentals — the first real programming course in the degree. Strong performance here builds confidence for all future programming courses.

**Outline**

1. Problems and problem-solving: routine vs non-routine problems
2. Methods of solving computing problems: algorithms and heuristics
3. Solvable and unsolvable problems
4. Solution techniques: abstraction, brainstorming, trial and error, divide and conquer, root cause analysis
5. General problem-solving process
6. Solution formulation and design: flowchart, pseudocode, decision table, decision tree
7. Implementation, evaluation and refinement
8. Programming in C and Python

**Recommended textbooks**

- Python Crash Course — Eric Matthes
- Think Python: How to Think Like a Computer Scientist — Allen Downey

**How to pass**

- Areté has 12 full interactive Python modules for this course — use them from day one
- Never copy-paste code examples — type every line yourself so your fingers learn the syntax
- Solve at least one coding problem daily, even if small; consistency beats cramming
- Harvard CS50P (Introduction to Programming with Python) is free and excellent

### GST 121 — Nigerian Peoples and Culture

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/gst-121
- 2 units · 100 Level · Second Semester

An introduction to Nigeria's ethnic diversity, cultural heritage, colonial and political history, and nation-building challenges. Provides context for the social and policy dimensions of technology in Nigeria.

**Outline**

1. Nigerian history, culture and art up to 1800 (Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo, and minority groups)
2. Nigeria under colonial rule and colonial administration
3. Evolution of Nigeria as a political unit: amalgamation, nationalist movement, independence
4. Challenges of nation-building: military intervention, the Nigerian Civil War
5. Trade and economics of self-reliance: indigenous trade, apprenticeship, skill acquisition
6. Social justice, national development, and the judiciary
7. Individual norms and values; citizenship acquisition and civic responsibilities
8. Re-orientation and national values: the 3Rs and national orientation strategies

**Recommended textbooks**

- Nigerian Peoples and Culture — Emmanuel N. Emeka
- The History of Nigeria — Toyin Falola

**How to pass**

- Link course topics to current events — Nigerian news puts everything in context
- For the culture component, draw on your own background and community knowledge
- Cybercrime and digital-policy topics connect directly to computing degrees — pay extra attention there
- Past questions drive most of the exam content for GST courses — collect and study them

### MTH 121 — General Mathematics II (Calculus)

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/mth-121
- 2 units · 100 Level · Second Semester

Single-variable calculus: limits, continuity, differentiation, integration, and their applications. Builds the analytical foundation for probability, statistics, and the signal theory used across science and engineering.

**Outline**

1. Functions of a real variable: domain, range, composition
2. Limits, continuity, and the derivative
3. Rules of differentiation: product, quotient, chain
4. Implicit, parametric, exponential and logarithmic differentiation
5. Applications of derivatives: tangents, rates, max/min
6. Definite and indefinite integrals
7. Techniques of integration: substitution, by parts, partial fractions
8. Applications of integration: area, volume

**Recommended textbooks**

- Engineering Mathematics — K.A. Stroud
- Calculus: Early Transcendentals — James Stewart

**How to pass**

- 3Blue1Brown "Essence of Calculus" on YouTube builds genuine geometric intuition — watch it
- Calculus rewards consistent daily practice more than any last-minute cramming
- Understand the concept of a derivative as 'rate of change' before memorising rules
- Khan Academy calculus is free, self-paced, and covers this entire course

### PHY 121 — General Physics II (Electricity & Magnetism)

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/phy-121
- 2 units · 100 Level · Second Semester

Electrostatics, DC circuits, magnetism, and electromagnetic induction. The electromagnetic foundations of this course directly underpin networking, wireless communications, and electronics studied in later years.

**Outline**

1. Electrostatics: electric charge, Coulomb's law and superposition
2. Electric field and potential; Gauss's law; capacitance; electric dipoles
3. Conductors, insulators, and energy in electric fields
4. DC circuits: current, voltage, resistance, Ohm's law, resistor combinations
5. Magnetic fields: Lorentz force, Biot-Savart and Ampère's laws, magnetic dipoles
6. Electromagnetic induction: Faraday and Lenz's laws, self and mutual inductance
7. Transformers and Maxwell's equations
8. Electromagnetic oscillations and waves; AC voltages and currents in inductors, capacitors, and resistors

**Recommended textbooks**

- University Physics with Modern Physics — Young & Freedman
- Fundamentals of Physics — Halliday, Resnick & Walker

**How to pass**

- Connect electricity topics to real circuits: every concept has a practical application
- Draw circuit diagrams before applying Kirchhoff's laws — never solve blind
- AC circuit analysis uses complex numbers from MTH — revise those in parallel
- MIT OCW 8.02 Electricity and Magnetism lectures are free and excellent

### PHY 128 — General Practical Physics II

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/phy-128
- 1 unit · 100 Level · Second Semester

Laboratory practicals continuing from PHY 117, covering the theoretical concepts of PHY 121 through quantitative measurement, treatment of measurement errors, and graphical analysis.

**Outline**

1. Continuation of quantitative measurement techniques from PHY 117
2. Treatment of measurement errors
3. Graphical analysis of experimental data
4. Electricity and magnetism experiments
5. Data collection and tabulation of observations
6. Numerical and graphical analysis, drawing conclusions from data
7. Preparation and presentation of practical reports

**Recommended textbooks**

- Practical Physics — G.L. Squires
- Physics Laboratory Manual — Loyd

**How to pass**

- Arrive at every practical knowing the theory — lab demonstrators mark understanding, not just results
- Record ALL raw readings in your lab notebook before doing any calculations
- Always quote uncertainties with your measurements — it demonstrates scientific rigour
- Submit lab reports on time; late submissions lose marks even when the content is perfect

### UUY-CYB 121 — Introduction to Computer Networks

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-cyb-121
- 2 units · 100 Level · Second Semester

Foundational networking: how data travels across local and wide area networks, the OSI/TCP-IP models, IP addressing and subnetting, routing protocols, and simulation with Packet Tracer. Critical groundwork for network security courses in later years.

**Outline**

1. Fundamentals of computer networks: LAN/MAN/WAN, Internet, Intranet, Extranet
2. Network topology, devices, and modes of data transmission
3. Network architecture: peer-to-peer, client-server, WLAN and IEEE standards
4. OSI reference model and TCP/IP protocol suite; physical and link layer functionalities
5. LAN technologies: Ethernet, Token Ring, multiple access schemes (CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA), MAC addressing
6. Network layer: IP, ARP, ICMP; IPv4 addressing and subnetting; routing protocols (RIP, OSPF, BGP)
7. Transport layer: UDP and TCP, ports and sockets, connection establishment, flow/congestion control
8. Application layer protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS, SMTP, TELNET) and IPv6 transition

**Recommended textbooks**

- Computer Networks — Andrew S. Tanenbaum & David J. Wetherall
- CompTIA Network+ Study Guide — Todd Lammle

**How to pass**

- Memorise the 7 OSI layers and what happens at each — this appears in every networking exam
- Practice subnetting until it is instinctive: it reappears in Network Defense and Security courses
- Professor Messer's free Network+ course on YouTube is one of the best networking courses available
- Use Cisco Packet Tracer (free) to simulate and visualise network configurations hands-on

### UUY-CYB 122 — Principles and Practice of Information Security

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-cyb-122
- 2 units · 100 Level · Second Semester

An introduction to the core principles of information security: operating system protection mechanisms, intrusion detection, formal security models, cryptography and steganography, and the policy/regulatory dimension of protecting information and value across networks.

**Outline**

1. Operating system protection mechanisms
2. Intrusion detection systems
3. Formal models of security
4. Cryptography and steganography
5. Network and distributed system security
6. Transfer of funds/value across networks; electronic voting security
7. Secure application design
8. Homeland cybersecurity policy and government regulation of information technology

**Recommended textbooks**

- Principles of Information Security — Michael E. Whitman & Herbert J. Mattord
- CompTIA Security+ Study Guide — Mike Chapple & David Seidl

**How to pass**

- The CIA triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) is the lens through which every security concept is understood — internalise it
- Read real breach case studies (Troy Hunt's blog, Krebs on Security) — they make abstract threats concrete
- Professor Messer's free Security+ course covers most of this curriculum and is excellent
- Social engineering is the most common attack vector — understand human psychology, not just technical controls
- Scope triage: the examinable core is what was actually lectured — Lectures 1–4, which are sections 7–12 of the lecture notes (Whitman & Mattord chapters 1–4). Cryptography/steganography and funds transfer/e-voting sit in the course outline but were never taught, so revise them last if at all
- Written paper, not CBT: a 10-mark question wants roughly five distinct points, each named and then explained in a sentence or two. One long unbroken paragraph scores badly even when everything in it is correct — the marker is counting points
- Structure every long answer the same way: define the term, explain the mechanism, give an example or a diagram, then link it to a neighbouring concept. A repeatable skeleton stops you freezing on a question you half-know
- Practise reproducing the diagrams from memory with their labels — the McCumber Cube, the TCP three-way handshake, the SDLC waterfall, top-down vs bottom-up. "With the aid of a diagram" is a standard question stem and the labels are where the marks are
- On a four-from-six paper in two hours, budget about 30 minutes per question: 5 planning the points, 20 writing, 5 checking. Read all six and pick your four before you write a single word
- Where a list is long (the fifteen threat categories, for instance) the question will ask for "any five" — so learn five you can explain properly rather than fifteen you can only name

### UUY-CYB 123 — Web Authoring and Development

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-cyb-123
- 2 units · 100 Level · Second Semester

Building web pages from scratch: web architecture and the client-server model, HTML structure, CSS styling, JavaScript interactivity, and XML documents. An entry point into web security topics and the front-end layer targeted by many cybersecurity attacks.

**Outline**

1. Web programming basics: the Internet, WWW, and internet services/protocols
2. Web application architecture, the network model, and the web development life cycle
3. HTML: tags and attributes, page structure, lists, tables, and forms
4. CSS: basics, adding style to HTML, text/font/colour, borders, margin and padding
5. JavaScript: basics, arithmetic operators, control statements, event handlers
6. Extensible Markup Language (XML): basics, formatting, viewing, and validating documents
7. Introduction to web security: XSS, CSRF concepts

**Recommended textbooks**

- HTML and CSS: Design and Build Websites — Jon Duckett
- JavaScript: The Good Parts — Douglas Crockford

**How to pass**

- freeCodeCamp Responsive Web Design certification is free and covers exactly this curriculum
- Build at least one real web page per week — the only way to learn web development is to build
- Inspect real websites using browser DevTools (F12) to see how professional sites are structured
- Learn the web security concepts early — XSS and CSRF from this course appear in later security courses

### UUY-DTS 121 — Foundation of Web Technologies for Data Science

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-121
- 3 units · 100 Level · Second Semester

How the web works and how to get data out of it. HTML, CSS and JavaScript fundamentals, HTTP and APIs, and the beginnings of web scraping — because a great deal of the data you will ever analyse lives behind a URL.

**Outline**

1. Internet and web fundamentals: clients, servers, DNS, URLs and the request/response cycle
2. HTTP: methods, status codes, headers, cookies and sessions
3. HTML: document structure, semantic elements, lists, tables and forms
4. CSS: selectors, the box model, layout with flexbox and grid, responsive design
5. JavaScript basics: variables, control flow, functions, DOM manipulation and events
6. The Document Object Model as a data structure you can query
7. Web APIs and JSON: consuming a REST endpoint, parsing responses
8. Introduction to web scraping: HTML parsing, selectors, pagination, and the ethics and legality of scraping
9. Serving a simple data dashboard on the web

**Recommended textbooks**

- HTML and CSS: Design and Build Websites — Jon Duckett
- Eloquent JavaScript — Marijn Haverbeke
- Web Scraping with Python — Ryan Mitchell

**How to pass**

- Open dev tools (F12) on every site you visit and read the Network tab — you learn HTTP faster by watching it than by reading about it
- Focus your effort on the DOM and on APIs/JSON; those are the parts a data scientist uses weekly, unlike CSS layout
- Always check a site's robots.txt and terms before scraping, and rate-limit your requests — the ethics questions are examined and the habit matters professionally
- Build one small thing that fetches a public API and charts the result; it is the best possible revision for this course

### UUY-DTS 122 — Introduction to Information and Communication Management

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-122
- 3 units · 100 Level · Second Semester

How organisations create, move, store and govern information, and how ICT infrastructure supports that. The organisational context in which data work actually happens — systems, stakeholders, policy and communication.

**Outline**

1. Information concepts: data, information, knowledge and wisdom; the DIKW hierarchy
2. Information systems in organisations: TPS, MIS, DSS and executive information systems
3. The information lifecycle: creation, storage, retrieval, distribution, archiving and disposal
4. Communication models, channels and barriers in an organisational setting
5. ICT infrastructure: networks, servers, cloud services and collaboration platforms
6. Records and document management; metadata and classification
7. Information governance: quality, ownership, stewardship and retention policy
8. Data privacy and protection: NDPR, GDPR principles, and confidentiality obligations
9. Presenting information to non-technical stakeholders

**Recommended textbooks**

- Management Information Systems: Managing the Digital Firm — Laudon & Laudon
- Information Systems Today — Valacich & Schneider

**How to pass**

- Learn the NDPR basics properly — Nigerian data protection law is directly examinable here and again in DTS 318
- For every system type (TPS/MIS/DSS), memorise one concrete Nigerian example; scenario questions ask you to classify a system
- The communication half of this course is not filler: explaining a result to a non-technical manager is a graded skill in DTS 413 and a career-defining one after
- Draw the DIKW pyramid and the information lifecycle from memory — both are near-certain exam diagrams

## 200 Level

### COS 211 — Computer Programming I

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cos-211
- 3 units · 200 Level · First Semester

Object-oriented programming in Java: from variables and control flow through full OOP, collections, exception handling, file I/O, and GUI development with Swing. The primary programming course of the degree and the subject most likely to determine your programming competence throughout your career.

**Outline**

1. Programming paradigms: functional, declarative, logic, and object-oriented
2. Java syntax: variables, data types, expressions, operators
3. Control flow: if/else, switch, loops; arrays (1D and 2D)
4. Methods: parameters, return types, overloading
5. Classes and objects; abstraction, constructors and encapsulation
6. Inheritance, polymorphism, and abstract classes; interfaces
7. Exception handling: try, catch, finally, custom exceptions
8. Collections API: ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet, Stack, Queue, iterators/enumerators
9. Strings and string processing; searching, sorting, and recursive algorithms
10. Event-driven programming: event-handling methods and event propagation
11. File I/O: reading and writing text files; GUI programming with Java Swing
12. Basic JDBC: connecting Java to a database

**Recommended textbooks**

- Introduction to Java Programming and Data Structures — Y. Daniel Liang
- Head First Java — Kathy Sierra & Bert Bates

**How to pass**

- Areté has 13 full interactive modules for this course with live playgrounds and quizzes — use them every day
- Type every code example yourself; copying and pasting prevents your brain from building muscle memory
- Java OOP is the most exam-critical section — understand inheritance diagrams and method overriding
- The AI Tutor on this app can explain any Java concept or debug your code any time

### CYB 211 — Introduction to Cybersecurity and Strategy

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-211
- 2 units · 200 Level · First Semester

A strategic overview of the cybersecurity landscape: basic concepts (confidentiality, integrity, availability, authentication, non-repudiation), security policy and incident response, risk management, and the national/organisational strategies that guide security decision-making at scale.

**Outline**

1. Basic concepts: cyber, security, CIA, authentication, access control, non-repudiation
2. Security policies, best current practices, testing, and incident response
3. Risk management, disaster recovery, and access control
4. Basic cryptography and software application vulnerabilities; evolution of cyber-attacks
5. Operating system protection, IDS, formal security models, steganography, DoS/worms/viruses
6. Transfer of funds/value across networks and electronic voting security
7. Cybersecurity policy, guidelines, and government regulation of information technology
8. Main actors of cyberspace; impact on civil/military institutions, privacy, business, government
9. Ethical obligations of security professionals; standards and frameworks

**Recommended textbooks**

- Cybersecurity Essentials — Charles J. Brooks et al.
- The Art of Intrusion — Kevin Mitnick

**How to pass**

- Follow cybersecurity news (Krebs on Security, The Hacker News) — exam questions often reference current events
- Understand the cyber kill chain model deeply — it frames every attack and defence strategy in the field
- Nigeria's National Cybersecurity Policy is public and freely available — read the executive summary
- Link strategic concepts back to technical mechanisms from UUY-CYB 122 to build integrated understanding

### CYB 213 — Cybercrime, Law and Countermeasures

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-213
- 2 units · 200 Level · First Semester

The legal and regulatory landscape of cybercrime: Nigerian cybercrime law, international frameworks, types of cybercrime, investigative procedures, and technical countermeasures. Essential context for any cybersecurity professional.

**Outline**

1. Definition, types and categories of cybercrime; threats to national critical infrastructure
2. Investigation process and procedure for cybercrime; strategies of perpetrators and prevention
3. Technical aspects of cybercrime investigations; attacks and defences used by terrorists and criminals
4. Use of online social networks in cybercrime investigation
5. Computer and network forensics: concepts, trends, and methods
6. Digital evidence collection and evaluation
7. Legal issues, international jurisdiction, and privacy issues
8. Cyber law application internationally: Europe, North/South America, Asia
9. The cyber law framework in Nigeria (Cybercrime Act 2015, EFCC); challenges and opportunities for enforcement

**Recommended textbooks**

- Cybercrime and the Law — Susan W. Brenner
- Cybercrime: An Introduction to an Emerging Phenomenon — Joseph F. Donnermeyer

**How to pass**

- Download and read the actual Nigeria Cybercrime Act 2015 — it is short and publicly available
- Case studies of Nigerian cybercrime prosecution are in EFCC press releases — use them in exam answers
- Distinguish clearly between cybercrime as a tool, as a target, and as an environment
- Link every legal concept to a technical mechanism: knowing both sides earns the best marks

### DTS 211 — Introduction to R Programming

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-211
- 2 units · 200 Level · First Semester

R from the ground up: the language, its data structures, and the tidyverse workflow for importing, tidying, transforming, visualising and modelling data. R is the statistician's language, and it is the fastest route from a dataset to a publication-quality figure.

**Outline**

1. The R environment and RStudio; scripts, projects and the console
2. Atomic vectors, coercion and vectorised operations
3. Data structures: vectors, matrices, lists, factors and data frames
4. Control flow, functions and the apply family
5. Reading and writing data: CSV, Excel, delimited files and databases
6. The tidyverse: dplyr verbs (filter, select, mutate, arrange, summarise, group_by)
7. Tidy data principles and reshaping with tidyr
8. Visualisation with ggplot2: the grammar of graphics, aesthetics, geoms, facets and themes
9. Reproducible reporting with R Markdown / Quarto

**Recommended textbooks**

- R for Data Science — Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel & Garrett Grolemund
- The Art of R Programming — Norman Matloff

**How to pass**

- Install R and RStudio in week one and never read R code without running it
- Learn the six dplyr verbs cold — filter, select, mutate, arrange, group_by, summarise. Together they solve most real data-wrangling tasks
- ggplot2 feels strange until the grammar of graphics clicks: data → aesthetic mapping → geometry. Once it clicks it is faster than anything else
- Do everything in an R Markdown / Quarto document from the start so your work is reproducible — you will need exactly this for DTS 417

### DTS 212 — Introduction to Data Science

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-212
- 2 units · 200 Level · First Semester

The formal treatment of the data science process, building on UUY-DTS 111: problem formulation, data acquisition, feature construction, model families, evaluation, and the ethics and limits of inference from data.

**Outline**

1. Framing a data science problem: from a vague question to a measurable target
2. Data acquisition strategies and sampling; sampling bias and its consequences
3. Data cleaning and preparation: missing data mechanisms, imputation, outlier treatment
4. Feature engineering, encoding categorical variables, scaling and normalisation
5. Exploratory data analysis: distributions, relationships, and the grammar of graphics
6. Supervised vs unsupervised learning; regression vs classification
7. Model evaluation: train/test split, cross-validation, and the bias–variance trade-off
8. Overfitting, underfitting and regularisation as concepts
9. Communicating results; reproducibility and the ethics of data-driven claims

**Recommended textbooks**

- An Introduction to Statistical Learning — James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani
- Python Data Science Handbook — Jake VanderPlas

**How to pass**

- The bias–variance trade-off is the conceptual centre of this course and of the whole degree — be able to explain it with a picture, in words, and with a formula
- Never evaluate a model on data it was trained on. Internalise this now and it will save your final-year project
- Watch the free ISLR video lectures from the authors; they follow the book chapter by chapter
- For every technique, learn the assumption it makes and what breaks when the assumption fails — that is what distinguishes a data scientist from a button-pusher

### GST 211 — Philosophy, Logic and Human Existence

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/gst-211
- 2 units · 200 Level · First Semester

Philosophical method, formal logic, and the perennial questions about knowledge, value and human existence. The logic half is directly technical — it is the same propositional calculus you will formalise in MTH 212 and implement in code.

**Outline**

1. The meaning, scope and branches of philosophy
2. Philosophy and logic: the nature of argument, premises and conclusions
3. Deductive and inductive reasoning; validity, soundness and cogency
4. Symbolic logic: propositions, connectives, truth tables and truth-functional analysis
5. Rules of inference and methods of proof
6. Informal fallacies: ad hominem, straw man, false cause, hasty generalisation, appeal to authority
7. Epistemology: sources and limits of knowledge; scepticism
8. Ethics: consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics
9. Human existence, freedom, determinism and the meaning of life

**Recommended textbooks**

- Philosophy and Logic: An Introduction — Various UniUyo GST course team
- A Concise Introduction to Logic — Patrick J. Hurley

**How to pass**

- Truth tables are free marks — practise until you can build one for any compound proposition without hesitating
- The fallacies section is the most examined: learn each one with a one-line example you invented yourself, not the textbook's
- Statistical reasoning is inductive; understanding why induction can never give certainty makes DTS 224 hypothesis testing click
- For essay questions, define your terms in the first paragraph — examiners reward it explicitly

### GST 212 — Philosophy, Logic and Human Existence

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/gst-212
- 2 units · 200 Level · First Semester

An examination of philosophical reasoning, formal logic, and the human condition. The logic component — syllogism, symbolic logic, and rules of inference — directly supports discrete mathematics and the formal reasoning used in security proofs and algorithm design.

**Outline**

1. Scope, notions, meanings, branches and problems of philosophy
2. Logic as an indispensable tool of philosophy
3. Elements of syllogism and symbolic logic; the first nine rules of inference
4. Informal fallacies, laws of thought, and the nature of arguments
5. Valid and invalid arguments; logic of form vs logic of content
6. Deduction, induction, and inference; creative and critical thinking
7. Impact of philosophy on human existence and conduct
8. Philosophy and politics, religion, human values, and character moulding

**Recommended textbooks**

- Introduction to Logic — Irving M. Copi & Carl Cohen
- Philosophy: The Basics — Nigel Warburton

**How to pass**

- The logic component matters most for your degree — practise truth tables until they are automatic
- Logical validity and logical truth are different concepts — do not confuse them in exams
- Ethical technology topics (privacy, AI, cybercrime) connect directly to your computing courses
- Argument mapping: writing out premises and conclusions explicitly prevents exam errors

### MTH 211 — Mathematical Methods I

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/mth-211
- 2 units · 200 Level · First Semester

The analytical toolkit for scientific computing: sequences and series, partial differentiation, vector calculus and an introduction to differential equations. These are the methods that underpin optimisation, gradient-based learning and statistical modelling.

**Outline**

1. Sequences and infinite series; tests of convergence
2. Power series, Taylor and Maclaurin expansions
3. Functions of several variables; limits and continuity in several variables
4. Partial derivatives; the chain rule for multivariable functions
5. Total differential, gradient, directional derivative, divergence and curl
6. Maxima and minima of functions of several variables; Lagrange multipliers
7. Multiple integrals: double and triple integrals and their applications
8. First-order ordinary differential equations: separable, homogeneous, exact and linear
9. Second-order linear differential equations with constant coefficients

**Recommended textbooks**

- Advanced Engineering Mathematics — Erwin Kreyszig
- Engineering Mathematics — K.A. Stroud

**How to pass**

- The gradient is THE central object of machine learning — every training algorithm you meet in UUY-DTS 313 is gradient descent on a loss surface. Learn it here properly and that course becomes much easier
- Lagrange multipliers are constrained optimisation, which is exactly what a support vector machine solves — the connection is not decorative
- Taylor series is how numerical methods approximate everything; MTH 223 next semester assumes you have it cold
- Practise partial differentiation until you stop confusing it with total differentiation — that specific mistake costs marks every year

### MTH 212 — Sets, Logic and Algebra

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/mth-212
- 2 units · 200 Level · First Semester

Rigorous foundations: set theory, formal logic, relations and functions, and an introduction to abstract algebraic structures. This is where mathematical proof is taught properly, and where the language of the rest of your theoretical courses is set.

**Outline**

1. Set theory: operations, laws, power sets, Cartesian products, indexed families
2. Propositional logic: connectives, truth tables, tautologies, logical equivalence
3. Predicate logic: quantifiers, bound and free variables, negation of quantified statements
4. Methods of proof: direct proof, contraposition, contradiction, mathematical induction
5. Relations: reflexive, symmetric, transitive; equivalence relations and partitions
6. Partial orders, Hasse diagrams and lattices
7. Functions: injective, surjective, bijective; composition and inverse functions; cardinality
8. Binary operations and algebraic structures: groups, subgroups, cyclic groups
9. Rings and fields: definitions, examples and elementary properties

**Recommended textbooks**

- Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications — Kenneth H. Rosen
- Book of Proof — Richard Hammack

**How to pass**

- Proof is a skill, not knowledge — you must write proofs yourself, badly at first, to learn it. Reading proofs feels productive and is not
- Equivalence relations and partitions are the mathematical basis of clustering: a clustering is literally a partition of your dataset
- Learn to negate a quantified statement mechanically (¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x)) — it is examined and it is how you state a null hypothesis correctly
- Hammack's Book of Proof is free and will teach you more in three chapters than a term of passive lectures

### SEN 211 — Introduction to Software Engineering

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/sen-211
- 2 units · 200 Level · First Semester

The principles and practices of building software systematically: software development lifecycle models, requirements engineering, system design, testing, and project management. Context for how secure software is planned and built.

**Outline**

1. Software engineering concepts, principles, and its place as a computing discipline
2. Software processes: lifecycle and process models, process assessment and metrics
3. Software requirements, specifications, design, and architecture
4. Software quality, testing, and validation
5. Software evolution: maintenance, re-engineering, legacy systems, and software reuse
6. Software project management: team management, scheduling, estimation, risk analysis
7. Software quality assurance and configuration management
8. Version control with Git and GitHub
9. Software engineering and law; secure software development lifecycle

**Recommended textbooks**

- Software Engineering — Ian Sommerville
- Clean Code — Robert C. Martin

**How to pass**

- Learn Git now — it is used for every programming project in years 3 and 4
- UML diagrams appear heavily in exams: practise class and sequence diagrams until they are fast to draw
- Relate SDLC models to the projects you build in COS 211 — theory becomes concrete immediately
- The Secure SDLC section links directly to your cybersecurity courses — connect them explicitly

Covers the legal/ethical framework under which penetration testing operates.

The architecture, protocols, market segments, and security challenges of the Internet of Things. Covers sensing/actuation, cloud data collection and analysis, smart-city and industrial use cases, and the unique vulnerabilities of IoT devices — a rapidly growing attack surface.

Analytics as a business discipline: the four analytics types (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive), KPI design, dashboarding, and turning an analysis into a decision. Practical and tool-focused.

Advanced programming building on COS 211: deeper object-oriented programming (polymorphism, abstract classes, interfaces), the Collections API, searching/sorting/recursion, event-driven and GUI programming. Bridges programming skills and the algorithmic thinking required for security tool development.

### CSC 223 — Discrete Structures

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/csc-223
- 2 units · 200 Level · Second Semester

The mathematics of discrete objects — counting, graphs, trees, recurrence relations and Boolean algebra. Graph theory in particular is the direct foundation for network analysis, recommendation systems and the web-data work in UUY-DTS 311.

**Outline**

1. Review of sets, relations and functions in a computing context
2. Propositional and predicate logic; logical equivalence and inference
3. Proof techniques: induction and strong induction; recursive definitions
4. Counting: the product and sum rules, permutations, combinations, the pigeonhole principle
5. Binomial coefficients and combinatorial identities; inclusion–exclusion
6. Recurrence relations and their solution; the Master theorem informally
7. Graph theory: graphs, digraphs, degree, paths, cycles, connectivity
8. Graph representations (adjacency matrix and list), traversal, shortest paths, spanning trees
9. Trees: rooted trees, binary trees, traversal; Boolean algebra and logic circuit minimisation

**Recommended textbooks**

- Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications — Kenneth H. Rosen
- Discrete Mathematics with Applications — Susanna S. Epp

**How to pass**

- Counting problems are deceptively hard — do many, and always ask "does order matter?" and "is repetition allowed?" before choosing a formula
- Graph theory is the highest-value topic for a data scientist here: social networks, web link structures and recommendation graphs are all this
- Recurrence relations explain the running time of recursive algorithms from COS 221 — study the two courses together
- Rosen's exercises are the best preparation for the exam; work them rather than re-reading notes

### CYB 222 — Cybersecurity Innovation and New Technologies

Emerging technologies and their cybersecurity implications: AI in security, blockchain, quantum computing threats to cryptography, zero-trust architecture, and the innovation lifecycle in the security industry.

1. AI and machine learning in threat detection
2. Blockchain technology and its security properties
3. Quantum computing and the threat to current cryptography

7. Security innovation lifecycle and technology adoption
8. Open-source intelligence (OSINT) modern tools

**Recommended textbooks**

- Blockchain Basics — Daniel Drescher

**How to pass**

- Stay current — this course changes rapidly; subscribe to a cybersecurity newsletter (SANS, Dark Reading)
- Zero trust ("never trust, always verify") is a major industry direction — understand it thoroughly
- Quantum threats to RSA and AES connect directly to your Cryptography course in 300L
- For exam essays, structure answers around: what the technology is, its security benefit, and its risk

### CYB 224 — Information and Big Data Security

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-224

Big data fundamentals — characteristics, sources, platforms, and analytics — paired with the security side: information and big data security requirements, lifecycle security management, risk management, and cloud-based big data security.

3. Operational and analytical big data; business intelligence vs big data vs data mining

### DTS 224 — Statistical Inference and Modelling

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-224
- 3 units · 200 Level · Second Semester

Reasoning from a sample to a population: estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and the linear model. The core statistical machinery of the degree — and the part most often misused in practice.

**Outline**

1. Populations, samples, parameters and statistics; sampling distributions
2. The Central Limit Theorem and its practical consequences
3. Point estimation: unbiasedness, efficiency, consistency; method of moments and maximum likelihood
4. Interval estimation: confidence intervals for means, proportions and variances
5. Hypothesis testing: null and alternative hypotheses, test statistics, p-values, Type I and Type II errors, power
6. One- and two-sample tests: z, t, chi-square and F tests
7. Analysis of variance (ANOVA): one-way and two-way
8. Simple and multiple linear regression: estimation, interpretation, inference on coefficients
9. Model diagnostics: residual analysis, multicollinearity, and the assumptions of the linear model

**Recommended textbooks**

- Mathematical Statistics with Applications — Wackerly, Mendenhall & Scheaffer
- Statistical Inference — George Casella & Roger L. Berger
- OpenIntro Statistics — Diez, Çetinkaya-Rundel & Barr

**How to pass**

- Learn what a p-value actually is and — more importantly — what it is not. Almost everyone gets this wrong, and examiners specifically test the misinterpretations
- A confidence interval is a statement about the procedure, not about the parameter. Say it correctly once and it stays right forever
- Simulate the Central Limit Theorem yourself in R (DTS 211): draw 1000 samples, plot the means, watch it become normal. Nothing else makes it as concrete
- For every test, memorise the assumptions alongside the formula — "which test do I use here?" is the exam's favourite question

### DTS 226 — Probability for Data Science

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-226
- 3 units · 200 Level · Second Semester

The mathematics of uncertainty: probability axioms, random variables, distributions, expectation, and the limit theorems. Probability is the language machine learning is written in — every model output is ultimately a probability statement.

**Outline**

1. Sample spaces, events and the axioms of probability
2. Conditional probability, independence, the law of total probability and Bayes' theorem
3. Discrete random variables: probability mass functions, expectation and variance
4. Discrete distributions: Bernoulli, binomial, geometric, hypergeometric, Poisson
5. Continuous random variables: density and distribution functions
6. Continuous distributions: uniform, exponential, gamma, normal
7. Joint, marginal and conditional distributions; covariance and correlation
8. Transformations of random variables; moment generating functions
9. Laws of large numbers and the Central Limit Theorem; introduction to Markov chains

**Recommended textbooks**

- A First Course in Probability — Sheldon Ross
- Introduction to Probability — Blitzstein & Hwang

**How to pass**

- Bayes' theorem is the most important single formula in the course — it is the entire basis of Naive Bayes classifiers and of Bayesian inference
- Watch Joe Blitzstein's Stat 110 lectures (free on YouTube); they are the best probability teaching available anywhere
- For each distribution, learn the story that generates it ("number of successes in n trials", "waiting time until first event") — then you never have to guess which one applies
- Draw the sample space for small problems. Most probability mistakes are modelling mistakes, not arithmetic mistakes

### MTH 223 — Introduction to Numerical Analysis

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/mth-223
- 2 units · 200 Level · Second Semester

How to compute answers to mathematical problems that have no closed-form solution, and how to know when the computed answer is wrong. Error, convergence and stability — the reason floating-point arithmetic sometimes betrays you.

**Outline**

1. Sources of error: round-off, truncation, and floating-point representation
2. Absolute, relative and percentage error; error propagation and conditioning
3. Solution of nonlinear equations: bisection, false position, Newton–Raphson, secant method
4. Convergence criteria and rates of convergence
5. Solution of linear systems: Gaussian elimination, LU decomposition, pivoting
6. Iterative methods: Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel
7. Interpolation: Lagrange and Newton divided-difference polynomials; spline interpolation
8. Numerical differentiation and integration: trapezoidal rule, Simpson's rules
9. Numerical solution of ordinary differential equations: Euler and Runge–Kutta methods

**Recommended textbooks**

- Numerical Analysis — Richard L. Burden & J. Douglas Faires
- Numerical Methods in Engineering with Python 3 — Jaan Kiusalaas

**How to pass**

- Implement every method in Python as you learn it — a method you have coded is a method you understand
- Newton–Raphson is the same algorithm family as gradient descent; recognising that makes UUY-DTS 313 far less mysterious
- Learn WHY floating-point comparison with == is unsafe; this single fact prevents a whole class of real bugs in data pipelines
- Exam questions usually ask for two or three iterations by hand — practise tabulating iterations neatly and carrying enough decimal places

### UUY-CYB 221 — Network Defense Fundamentals

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-cyb-221
- 2 units · 200 Level · Second Semester

Practical network security: identification/authentication/authorization, threat classification, firewalls, administrative/physical/technical controls, virtualization and cloud, wireless/mobile/IoT security, and cryptography/PKI. Builds directly on the networking foundation from UUY-CYB 121.

**Outline**

1. Network security fundamentals; identification, authentication and authorization
2. Classification of threats: malware, intrusions, denial of service
3. Fundamentals of firewalls and implementation approaches
4. Network security controls: administrative, physical, and technical
5. Virtualization and cloud computing security
6. Wireless network security, mobile device security, and IoT device security
7. Data security: cryptography and public key infrastructure (PKI)
8. Network traffic monitoring; basic network utilities (ipconfig, ping, tracert, netstat)

**Recommended textbooks**

- Network Security Essentials — William Stallings
- CompTIA CySA+ Study Guide — Mike Chapple & David Seidl

**How to pass**

- Install Wireshark (free) and capture your own network traffic — hands-on analysis builds intuition fast
- Use Cisco Packet Tracer (free) to build and defend virtual networks before exams
- Know the difference between IDS (detect only) and IPS (detect + block) — exam-critical
- Relate every defence mechanism to a specific attack from UUY-CYB 212 — show the attack/defence pairing

### UUY-CYB 222 — Web and Mobile Applications Security

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-cyb-222
- 2 units · 200 Level · Second Semester

Attacking and defending web and mobile applications. Covers the OWASP Top 10 in depth, secure coding practices for Java/Python/Kotlin/Swift, audit and QA testing, and mobile-specific threats on iOS and Android platforms.

**Outline**

1. The impact of the internet and web applications on the business world
2. Principles and strategies for the design and implementation of secure applications — writing software that makes it difficult for intruders to exploit security loopholes in applications/code
3. Secure program development for mobile (Android, iOS) and web
4. Delineation of web-based risks, common website attacks, weaknesses, and security best practices
5. Value and importance of vulnerability and security assessment for web and mobile applications
6. Attributes and qualities of secure coding practices
7. Role and importance of audit compliance and quality assurance testing for web/mobile applications
8. Next-generation challenges in securing web/mobile applications and data
9. Lifecycle approach to web/mobile application security

**Recommended textbooks**

- The Web Application Hacker's Handbook — Stuttard & Pinto
- Real-World Bug Hunting — Peter Yaworski

**How to pass**

- PortSwigger Web Security Academy is free and has labs for every OWASP Top 10 vulnerability — essential
- DVWA (Damn Vulnerable Web Application) is a free practice target you can run locally
- For every vulnerability, know: how it works, how to exploit it, and how to fix it
- Bug bounty write-ups on HackerOne and Bugcrowd are the best real-world case studies

### UUY-DTS 224 — Programming in Data Science

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-224
- 2 units · 200 Level · Second Semester

The working Python data stack: NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib and scikit-learn. Where the mathematics of the other 200 Level courses becomes code you can run on a real dataset.

**Outline**

1. The scientific Python ecosystem; notebooks, environments and package management
2. NumPy: ndarrays, dtypes, vectorisation, broadcasting, slicing and linear algebra routines
3. pandas: Series and DataFrame, indexing, selection and filtering
4. Data cleaning in pandas: missing values, type conversion, duplicates, string operations
5. Reshaping and combining data: groupby, pivot, melt, merge and concat
6. Time-series handling: datetime indexes, resampling and rolling windows
7. Visualisation with Matplotlib and Seaborn
8. An introduction to scikit-learn: the estimator API, fit/predict, pipelines
9. Writing reusable code: functions, modules, virtual environments and version control with Git

**Recommended textbooks**

- Python for Data Analysis — Wes McKinney
- Python Data Science Handbook — Jake VanderPlas

**How to pass**

- Learn groupby properly — the split-apply-combine pattern solves an astonishing share of real analysis tasks
- Write vectorised NumPy/pandas code rather than Python loops; on a large dataset the difference is minutes versus hours
- Keep every notebook in Git from day one. Reproducibility is a graded expectation by DTS 417
- Recreate a chart you have seen in a news article using Matplotlib; matching a real design teaches more than following a tutorial

## 300 Level

### CSC 319 — Artificial Intelligence

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/csc-319
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester

Foundations of AI: intelligent agents, search algorithms, knowledge representation, semantic networks, natural language processing, and expert systems. Directly relevant to AI-powered anomaly detection, prediction, and automated analysis across computing.

**Outline**

1. Overview, history, goals, types, branches and applications of AI
2. Intelligent agents: performance, faculties, rationality, environment, architectures
3. Search: general classes of AI search problems, techniques and strategies
4. Knowledge representation: predicate logic, non-monotonic logic, probabilistic reasoning
5. Semantic networks and frames
6. Natural language processing: syntactic and semantic structures
7. Expert systems: characteristics, components, types, development
8. Programming languages for AI; introduction to computer image recognition
9. Lab: Turing test, facial recognition, chatbots, spam detection, sentiment analysis, machine translation

**Recommended textbooks**

- Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach — Stuart Russell & Peter Norvig
- Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras, and TensorFlow — Aurélien Géron

**How to pass**

- Understand A* search intuitively by tracing it on a grid before studying the formal algorithm
- Connect AI to a concrete application in your own field in every exam answer — applied answers score higher
- Google's free Machine Learning Crash Course covers supervised/unsupervised ML at the right level
- AI ethics questions (bias, fairness) appear frequently — develop considered, referenced arguments

### CYB 311 — Cryptography Techniques, Algorithms and Applications

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-311
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester

The mathematical and algorithmic foundations of modern cryptography: symmetric and asymmetric cryptosystems, key management, hash functions, digital signatures, PKI, and protocol security. The theoretical backbone of all secure communications.

**Outline**

1. Introduction to cryptography: symmetric and asymmetric cryptosystems, key management
2. Cryptanalysis; stream ciphers, block ciphers, and Feistel ciphers
3. Hash functions; data integrity, authentication, and perfect secrecy
4. Public-key cryptography and discrete algorithms: ElGamal, algorithmic number theory, primality testing
5. Security of ElGamal and RSA encryption; RSA key generation; discrete logarithm schemes
6. Selected cryptosystems: DES, RSA, and the AES symmetric block cipher
7. PKI, SSL, and VPN
8. Digital signatures, pseudo-random number generation, and cryptographic protocols
9. Certificate authorities; policies and procedures for the proper use of cryptography

**Recommended textbooks**

- Cryptography and Network Security — William Stallings
- Introduction to Modern Cryptography — Katz & Lindell

**How to pass**

- Work through RSA key generation by hand at least twice — the maths is not complex once you step through it
- Know the difference between confidentiality (encryption), integrity (MAC/hash), and authentication (signature)
- Computerphile on YouTube has outstanding, accessible videos on every topic in this course — free
- Quantum threats from this course directly link to CYB 222 (Innovation) and CYB 411 (Vulnerability Assessment)

### CYB 312 — Biometrics Security

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-312
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester

Biometric authentication systems: digital image/signal processing, matching algorithms, error metrics, and data security. Covers implementation in national identity systems and access control.

**Outline**

1. Introduction to biometrics and digital image processing
2. Biometric algorithms and systems: face, fingerprint, iris, voice
3. Automated biometric identification and multimodal biometrics
4. Biometric data: raw data, template data, and data methods
5. Matching basics: enrolment, match threshold, matching performance
6. Calculating error rates and graphs (FAR, FRR, EER)
7. Storage of biometric data: transactions, quality upgrades, data security and integrity
8. Privacy issues; security strength and recognition rates
9. Applications of biometrics and future trends; alternatives to passwords and smart cards

**Recommended textbooks**

- Introduction to Biometrics — Anil K. Jain, Arun A. Ross & Karthik Nandakumar
- Biometric System and Data Analysis — Ted Dunstone & Neil Yager

**How to pass**

- FAR vs FRR trade-off is the most examined concept — understand the EER graphically
- Nigeria's NIN (National Identity Number) system is a real-world case study for national biometrics
- Biometric privacy connects to the Nigeria Data Protection Act from CYB 224 — link them
- Presentation attack / spoofing scenarios make excellent exam answers for "practical examples"

### CYB 313 — Cybersecurity Risks Analysis, Challenges and Mitigation

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-313
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester

Systematic methods for identifying, analysing, and treating cybersecurity risks. Covers applied information security management, risk mitigation in the cloud, governance and security policy, the ISO 27000 series, and the economic/geopolitical factors behind Africa's cyber risk exposure.

**Outline**

1. Principles of applied information security management
2. Cybersecurity risks, challenges, and the path forward; recognizing risks
3. Decision and risk analysis techniques; mitigating risks and vulnerabilities
4. Effective use of assessments for cybersecurity risk mitigation, including in the cloud
5. Economic and geopolitical factors behind Africa's vulnerability to cyber-attacks
6. Governance and security policy; threat and vulnerability management
7. Incident management, risk assessment and risk management frameworks
8. Information leakage, crisis management, and business continuity
9. ISO 27000 series and the Plan-Do-Check-Act model
10. Incident response, forensics, and investigations; legal and regulatory drivers

**Recommended textbooks**

- Risk Analysis and the Security Survey — James F. Broder & Gene Tucker
- CompTIA Security+ Study Guide — Mike Chapple & David Seidl

**How to pass**

- Practise ALE/SLE/ARO calculations until they are automatic — they appear in nearly every exam
- STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, DoS, Elevation) — memorise and apply it to any system
- Risk registers are a practical exam task — practise building one for a sample organisation
- BCP and DR are distinct: BCP keeps the business running, DR recovers IT systems — know the difference

### DTS 312 — Big Data Computing

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-312
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester

What changes when the data no longer fits on one machine. Distributed storage and computation, the MapReduce model, Hadoop and Spark, and the architectural patterns of modern data platforms.

**Outline**

1. Characterising big data: volume, velocity, variety, veracity and value
2. Why scale-up fails and scale-out wins; commodity clusters and fault tolerance
3. Distributed file systems: HDFS architecture, blocks, replication, NameNode and DataNodes
4. The MapReduce programming model: map, shuffle, reduce; worked word-count and join examples
5. The Hadoop ecosystem: YARN, Hive, HBase, Sqoop, Flume
6. Apache Spark: RDDs, DataFrames, lazy evaluation, transformations vs actions, in-memory computation
7. Spark SQL and PySpark for data processing
8. Stream processing concepts: Kafka, windowing, and batch vs streaming architectures
9. NoSQL stores and the CAP theorem; cloud big-data services

**Recommended textbooks**

- Hadoop: The Definitive Guide — Tom White
- Learning Spark — Damji, Wenig, Das & Lee
- Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Martin Kleppmann

**How to pass**

- Be able to trace a word-count through map → shuffle → reduce by hand; it is the classic exam question and it teaches the model properly
- Install Spark locally (or use a free Databricks Community workspace) and run PySpark on a few million rows — the concepts stay abstract until you see a job execute
- Understand WHY Spark is faster than MapReduce (in-memory, DAG scheduling, lazy evaluation) rather than just asserting it
- The CAP theorem is examined nearly every year: know what each letter means and why you can only have two

### DTS 314 — Data Management I

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-314
- 3 units · 300 Level · First Semester

Database systems for the data professional, going well beyond UUY-DTS 112: advanced SQL, indexing and query performance, transactions and concurrency, and the design of data models that survive real workloads.

**Outline**

1. Review of the relational model and relational algebra
2. Advanced SQL: window functions, common table expressions, recursive queries, set operations
3. Views, stored procedures, triggers and user-defined functions
4. Physical design: storage structures, indexing (B-tree, hash), and when an index hurts
5. Query processing and optimisation; reading an execution plan
6. Transactions: ACID properties, concurrency control, locking, isolation levels and deadlock
7. Recovery, backup strategies and write-ahead logging
8. Database security: privileges, roles, injection prevention and encryption at rest
9. Distributed databases and NoSQL families: key-value, document, column-family and graph stores

**Recommended textbooks**

- Database System Concepts — Silberschatz, Korth & Sudarshan
- SQL Performance Explained — Markus Winand

**How to pass**

- Window functions are the highest-leverage SQL skill you can learn at this level — running totals, rankings and period-over-period comparisons all become one query
- Run EXPLAIN on your slow queries and read the plan. Knowing why a query is slow is a rarer skill than writing SQL at all
- Learn the isolation levels with the anomaly each one permits (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom) — that table is a standing exam question
- Practise on a database with at least a million rows; performance concepts are invisible on toy data

### DTS 318 — Ethics and Legal Issues in Data Science

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-318
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester

The obligations that come with holding and modelling data about people: privacy law, consent, algorithmic fairness, transparency and accountability. The course that determines whether your technical skill does good or harm.

**Outline**

1. Ethical frameworks applied to data: consequentialist, deontological and virtue perspectives
2. Privacy: informational self-determination, consent, purpose limitation and data minimisation
3. Anonymisation, pseudonymisation and re-identification risk; k-anonymity and differential privacy in outline
4. Data protection law: the Nigeria Data Protection Act, the NDPR, and the GDPR as a comparator
5. Rights of data subjects: access, rectification, erasure, portability and objection
6. Algorithmic bias and fairness: sources of bias, fairness metrics, and their trade-offs
7. Transparency, explainability and the right to an explanation; black-box models in high-stakes decisions
8. Accountability, auditing, and the governance of automated decision-making
9. Professional codes of conduct and case studies of data science failures

**Recommended textbooks**

- Weapons of Math Destruction — Cathy O'Neil
- Ethics and Data Science — Loukides, Mason & Patil
- Fairness and Machine Learning — Barocas, Hardt & Narayanan

**How to pass**

- Know the Nigeria Data Protection Act and the NDPR specifically — Nigerian law is what you are examined on and what will actually govern your work
- Learn why the different fairness metrics are mathematically incompatible; "just make it fair" is not an available option and examiners want you to know that
- Prepare three real case studies (e.g. COMPAS, a credit-scoring case, a facial-recognition case) in enough detail to analyse rather than merely name
- This is the course whose content you will most often actually need after graduation — treat it as professional training, not a compliance box

### GST 311 — Peace and Conflict Resolution

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/gst-311
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester

The nature of conflict, the conditions for peace, and the practical machinery of resolution — negotiation, mediation and arbitration. Applied to the Nigerian and West African context.

**Outline**

1. Basic concepts: peace, conflict, violence, security and human security
2. Types and causes of conflict: economic, political, ethnic, religious and resource conflict
3. Theories of conflict and conflict dynamics; conflict escalation and de-escalation
4. Peace as a process: peacekeeping, peacemaking, peacebuilding and peace enforcement
5. Conflict resolution mechanisms: negotiation, mediation, conciliation, arbitration and adjudication
6. Alternative dispute resolution (ADR) and traditional African conflict-resolution systems
7. The role of government, civil society, NGOs and international bodies (UN, AU, ECOWAS)
8. Case studies of conflict and resolution in Nigeria and West Africa
9. Developing a culture of peace; the role of the media and of data in early warning

**Recommended textbooks**

- Peace and Conflict Studies — David P. Barash & Charles P. Webel
- Introduction to Peace and Conflict Resolution — UniUyo GST course team

**How to pass**

- Learn the resolution mechanisms as a ladder from least to most binding (negotiation → mediation → arbitration → adjudication); scenario questions ask you to pick the right rung
- Have two Nigerian case studies fully prepared — specificity is what separates an A from a C in the essay
- Conflict early-warning systems are increasingly data-driven; mentioning that connection is a genuine differentiator in your answers
- This is another GST course of easy marks; do the past questions rather than over-reading

### GST 312 — Peace and Conflict Resolution

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/gst-312
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester

The causes, dynamics, and resolution of conflict in a multi-ethnic nation: types and theories of conflict, root causes of conflict and violence in Africa, peacebuilding strategies, and the roles of international organisations, media, and traditional institutions.

**Outline**

1. Concepts of peace, conflict, and security in a multi-ethnic nation
2. Types and theories of conflict: ethnic, religious, economic, geo-political
3. Root causes of conflict and violence in Africa; selected conflict case studies
4. Peacebuilding, management of conflicts and security
5. Insurgency and terrorism; peace mediation and peacekeeping
6. Alternative Dispute Resolution: dialogue, arbitration, negotiation, collaboration
7. Roles of international organisations: UN, African Union, ECOWAS
8. Media and traditional institutions in peacebuilding
9. Managing post-conflict situations: refugees, IDPs, and the role of NGOs

**Recommended textbooks**
